Dusi Disaster

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The worst disaster in more than 3 decades -- can the Dusi river recover from a devastating caustic soda and oil spill?

Unique Selling Point:
At 4am on the 13th of August a storage tank filled with cooking oil crumbled, taking down with it a second container filled with caustic soda. This happened at the Willowton Plant in Pietermaritzburg, KZN. The alkaline mix flowed down the Bain spruit and into the Dusi river. It is estimated that 1.6 million litres of oil and caustic soda ended up in the river and by the weekend the milky polluted water had entered the Inanda dam outside Durban. The liquid is suffocating fish and other aquatic animals. The water is undrinkable for the communities and their animals. According to environmentalists it will take the Dusi several decades to recover.

Summary:
The Mzunduzi (Dusi) river is famous because of the canoe marathon that is held on the river each year. It is the biggest canoeing event on the African continent, and one of the world’s most popular river marathons, attracting between 1600 and 2000 paddlers each year. But the river has also often been in the news for other reasons. Water quality has often been an issue and high e.coli counts are regularly measured. There are many rural communities who live along the banks of the river between PMB and Durban. On Tuesday 13 Aug there was a large oil and caustic soda spillage in PMB at the Willowton factory. 1.6 million litres of pollutants entered the Bain spruit and flowed into the Dusi river. The pollutants have had a devastating effect on the river, fish and other animals that depend on it. There are reports of dying cattle and massive fish die-offs all the way downstream to the Inanda dam.Provincial Government has issued a warning saying that people and animals should stay clear of the river. No-one should drink from the river, use it for irrigation or even paddle on it. The spill has been labelled the worst in 30 years. The Dusi Marathon organisers are concerned about the long-term effects on the river. The Dusi Umgeni Conservation Trust has stepped in to help monitor the water quality and assist in clean-up operations. Willowton has subcontracted 2 companies to help with the clean-up and government is also "working around the clock" but experts are saying that this kind of spill is very difficult to clean up. The caustic soda mixed with the oil has created a soapy substance that is suffocating all aquatic life in the river. Umgeni Water has tried to flush the river by opening the sluice of Henley Dam and although the water is running clear at some places, the damage has been done. Msunduzi Municipality spokesperson Thobeka Mafumbatha said the city’s environmental health unit was investigating the incident.

Further information:
Caustic soda is corrosive and can cause burns to living tissue. Combined with fatty oils it becomes soapy, making a river clean-up exceptionally difficult. Water specialist Dr Anthony Turton from the Centre for Environmental Management at the University of Free State said the clean-up could take several years if the pollution spreads all the way down to Inanda Dam. Another leading environmental consultant and river specialist, Pandora Long, agreed. Nearly all aquatic life in a conservancy area along the river has been wiped out, according to Long. Turton says water-use licences for industrial users requires the use of berms or bunds to contain spills of hazardous liquids, as well as formal reporting to the regulating authorities at specified intervals along with site inspections. “This incident provides evidence of failure of the regulatory process,” said Turton.

DUSI DISASTER SCRIPT

UPSOUND This is what it looks like today at the Dusi river, at Faraway farm… I’ll get a bit closer and you can see just the amount of fish that have died off and are continuing to die and wash downstream.

Our river is very dirty at the moment. We live here and we canoe here, so it’s very dangerous. Please people must stay away from the river.

Andrea Kotze Late in the afternoon I went down to my river and the smell of soap was just insane. You couldn’t breathe. And when I went closer I actually saw that the water was a grey colour.

Maureen Henson Thousands of dead fish floating on the river or caught up in the reeds. And the stench was horrific.
Sibusiso Ntinga They are crying saying that they are largely affected, badly with this pollution.

Tonia Long I arrived here on Saturday to absolute devastation. I think I was in shock for a few days. Now I think it’s starting to sink in, just the absolute death of our river.

V/o:On Tuesday the 13th of August, the Umzinduzi river in KZN was flooded with more than 1.5 million litres of caustic soda mixed with vegetable oil from an accidental industrial spill in Pietermaritzburg.
Pandora Long Derek: Pandora, what actually happened here?

They killed the river.
Like so many communities living along the banks of this iconic river, the Mpushini Valley community is still coming to terms with the fact that their river has been devastated.

Pandora Long The fish couldn’t breathe. It was like hugely alkalinic, the water. It was like 13.5 or something. And they started to climb out of the water. By Saturday there was just this sea of dead fish.

V/O: Pandora Long and her family have been living in the valley for decades and for them the tragedy is almost too much to bear.

Pandora Long The stench everywhere up the river. It’s sickening.

LINK:This is the origin of the spill, the Willowton edible oil processing factory in Pietermaritzburg. The deadly combination of oil and caustic soda flooded into a tributary called the Baynespruit and then into the Umzinduzi, or Dusi river.

V/O:From Maritzburg the river flows down towards Durban and meets up with the Umngeni before reaching Indian Ocean….

Willowton declined an on-camera interview, but according to their email correspondence, a vegetable oil storage tank collapsed and, in the process, brought down an adjacent tank filled with caustic soda. Two other tanks were damaged in the process. A detailed independent investigation is underway to establish the exact cause of the collapse.

Dave Still: They contained a good deal of it on the site but then a lot got off the site, into the river, into the sewage works and that’s had a pretty serious knock on the river for a long way down.

V/O: Dave Still is the chair of an NGO called DUCT - the Dusi Umgeni Conservation Trust - that has been championing the river and monitoring the water quality of the Dusi since its inception in 2005...

Dave Still: The level of sewage pollution in the Dusi - in this body of water here for example - the average is 5x higher now than it was 30 years ago. So, the long-term trend is very worrying.

V/O: The spilt chemicals made their way down the river, approximately 80kms downstream to the Inanda dam killing thousands of tonnes of fish - leaving a trail of devastation...

Dr Mark Graham It was just one of those rare coincidences where we had the mixture of oil and caustic soda and we get saponification and that process, for the chemists out there, and that’s really just how we make soap - oil and strong alkaline - and the soapy mixture landed up in the water and unfortunately that just affected the life living in the river.

V/O: Specialist Aquatic Scientist and independent consultant, Dr Mark Graham was appointed by Willowton to monitor the Dusi and determine the extent of the damage.
Dr Mark Graham In terms of aquatic life there has certainly been a significant impact so far. We’ve been looking at all the aspects of the aquatic life from the fish at the top of the food chain as it were, in the aquatic ecosystem, all the way down to little aquatic insects that they’d be feeding on and likewise the diatoms and algae that the invertebrates would be feeding on.

V/O: A quick sample of the water insects amongst the rocks and sediment says a lot...
Dr Mark Graham For a typical river like this you’d see…

Derek: You’d see more…

You’d see a hang of a lot more. So the fact that we’re seeing very few and very pollution tolerant families at this point is an indication of the kind of impacts that we’ve got on this system.

V/O: Willowton also employed the services of 2 pollution response companies to assist with the clean-up of the spill.
Dr Mark Graham Derek: What is being done to clean up the river?

Derek, there’s a huge amount of effort that has gone in and I’ve seen the evidence of that. Huge amounts of booms being put in place, materials added to the water to soak up particularly the oil material. As you can see here most of that has been removed at this stage.

V/O A huge part of the clean-up has been removing the dead fish from the river to help curb the further contamination of the water.

Dave Still The fish themselves, you know some people think the fish are poisonous, that’s not really the case. If you ate a fish that had just died it would be actually fine, but you don’t want rotting fish all the way down the catchment. That’s why they’re collecting them.

LINK: Just one of the thousands of fish that didn’t make it. Clearly past it’s sell-by date. Be grateful you don’t have smell-o-vision.

V/O The Dusi river is perhaps best known for Africa’s biggest canoe race, attracting around 2,000 paddlers each year.
Ray de Vries If something goes wrong in the river we’ll know about it first because a paddler will let us know.

V/o: Spokesperson for the Dusi Canoe Marathon, Ray de Vries says the event is an important annual money-spinner.

Ray de Vries: The Dusi is responsible, from an economic impact point of view to the region between 75 and 100 million bucks. That’s a lot of money that’s being spent there.

V/O: According to De Vries this spill could have an impact on the event.
Ray de Vries. The whole of Europe is talking about the spill, the media has reached that far. So from an international paddler point of view, that’s going to affect us. From a sponsorship view it affects us. Now is sponsorship season. I’m negotiating sponsors as we speak and everybody as put it on hold. Let’s just see how this plays out before we commit to anything.

LINK: The Dusi is famous for the annual Canoe race but what is more important is the effect on the community that lines it’s banks for many kilometres. In many ways this river is their lifeblood.

Ray de Vries You know the Dusi river is 160kms between Pietermaritzburg and Durban. There’s a million people that live over there. Lots and lots of people. We call them the forgotten communities. They’re the last people to find out when something goes wrong.

Sibosisu Their livestock, some showed us they’re dying along the river because they drank this water. They had no other option except to have this kind of water as they rely on the river.

V/O: Sibosisu Ntinga works closely with DUCT and assists with monitoring the Dusi river in the more rural areas. He says the people of villages like Nkanyezini are severely affected by the spill in the river.

In their gardens they’re now complaining saying that their vegetables, as they put water on, are now starting dying. They’re showing illness from this dirty water.

DORIS: Lucky You know, Derek, this has been a shock to our community. Especially because this is a rural area. Our people depend a lot on getting information when disasters like this take place.

V/O Lucky Dlamini is the spokesperson for the Kwa-Ximba conservancy that was established in 2013 to help protect the biodiversity of the area.
Lucky Derek: Has the government done much to spread the word?

There’s a lot happening but you still feel that there’s not enough information on the ground. We think that our Environmental Affairs department should be doing something. They should be with us on the ground all the time.

LINK: All fingers point to the KZN Department of the environment who should be standing up telling the affected community and the media about this spill and what is being done about it.

V/O But the information is not forthcoming, and they only sent us a pre-recorded video statement by the KZN MEC for Economic Development, Tourism and Environmental Affairs, filmed earlier last week.

Nomusa Dube-Ncube: We’ve heard about the unfortunate incident of spillage in the Umzinduzi river. We want to make sure that there has been compliance with the rules of the environmental act and we’ll ensure that those rules are adhered to. If there is any breach in terms of compliance we will have to make sure that whomever has breached the compliance will have to be fined or will have to be charged

V/O: In Willowton’s written response the state that: We deeply regret the accident, and as is our responsibility we are doing everything possible to contain, clean-up and remediate the affected environment and assist the impacted community.

V/O: In the meantime, the big question is how long will it take for the river to recover. There is talk of restocking the river, but Graham believes that given time the ecosystem might prove to be resilient...

Dr Mark Graham What we are looking at it what are the tributaries going to give us which haven’t been impacted that we can actually utilise and inoculum back into the system to bring life back into this river.
Dr Mark Graham Derek: Mark, spotlight on the Dusi, but surely nationally it’s just becoming a crisis with our rivers getting polluted?

It’s an absolute crisis Derek and I think these sort of incidents bring the focus on it but what we need is a longer term solution.

Dave Still Worldwide urban river are a big threat. Some countries are getting it right - others not so much. So, it’s a big challenge. Compared to some of the environmental problems in the world this is one of the more solvable ones. It’s really just a case of priorities and political will.

PROMO 1 11” A massive ACCIDENTAL toxic spill into the Dusi river in KZN, has killed thousands of tonnes of fish and shocked the local communities. What is the future of the Dusi?

PROMO 2 11” THE ACCIDENTAL SPILLAGE OF 1.6 million litres of vegetable oil and caustic soda into the iconic Dusi, has left communities in shock, and the future of the river in the balance.

PROMO 3 11” Thousands of tonnes of dead fish have been removed from the Umzimduzi river in KZN following an ACCIDENTAL industrial spill. Who will take responsibility for this disaster?





Pandora Long The human connections to rivers is far more deep than just ecologies, we are connected through an ecological cycle. Everything we do ends up in the river, it’s our water that we drink, but deeper than that it’s our cultural connection. The ceremony we have like our picnic is similar to ceremonies that they have in zulu cultures, celebrating life, celebrating the river...

Dr Mark Graham This is a little symptom and a pimple on the surface which has just burst and created all this interest, but really as a community, as a society we want to be looking at the longer, bigger picture… and sustainably.

Dr Mark Graham He’s collected a sample here from the stones insects. And he’s now just transferring that sample into a tray and we’re going to look and see what aquatic insect life is still in this river system.
Dr Mark Graham So like the fish and you and I, the aquatic life is very dependent on the dissolved oxygen in the water. So that’s available oxygen that they’re using for breathing. If there’s none of that they’re going to be highly impacted. A spill like this is often associated with the depletion of the oxygen and that is probably largely what we’re seeing by way of all the dead fish. So, we’re looking at the insects now to see how they are being affected by this as well.

Derek: And what have you found so far?

We’re finding impacted sites and certainly immediately downstream of the spill was a significant reduction in life. Jean, I think there was one Olego Keat… one of the leeches. So, it’s a leech - a tough as old boots aquatic life form - often associated with highly polluted water. And that was the only thing that was alive.
Dr Mark Graham What most people don’t realise is the complexity… we appreciate the wildlife at the game reserve when we see the grass and we see the wildebeest and so on - elephants and tigers and lions… But it’s exactly that same ecosystem that we’ve got here in the water and many things feeding on each other and being dependent on each other. So if one of those components is eliminated it has a cascade effect through the aquatic food web.


Dave Still Being a big industry, doing the kind of work they do they’ve always been quite a high risk. And it’s one of the industries that does from time to time I think affect the sewage plant.
Dave Still With the spill, some of that effluent went down the sewers, and the nature, being the caustic and the oils … that would have given the natural processes in the sewage plant a shock which basically give a big wow. After a few days I understand they’ve pretty much got it back right again. It hit it pretty hard for a few days.

Derek: Could’ve been far worse?

Yes it could have been.

Ray de Vries

Derek: Ray, what does the Dusi river mean to the people living in the valley?


Ray de Vries: The Dusi unfortunately is synonymous with Dusi guts and bad water and all the rest. Maritzburg is just a seeping sewer and that’s where all the big problem is.

LINK: Just one of the thousands of fish that didn’t make it. Clearly past it’s sell-by date. Be grateful you don’t have smell-o-vision. V/O The Dusi river is perhaps best known for Africa’s biggest canoe race, attracting around 2,000 paddlers each year. Ray de Vries If something goes wrong in the river we’ll know about it first because a paddler will let us know. V/o: Spokesperson for the Dusi Canoe Marathon, Ray de Vries says the event is an important annual money-spinner. Ray de Vries: The Dusi is responsible, from an economic impact point of view to the region between 75 and 100 million bucks. That’s a lot of money that’s being spent there. V/O: According to De Vries this spill could have an impact on the event. Ray de Vries. The whole of Europe is talking about the spill, the media has reached that far. So from an international paddler point of view, that’s going to affect us. From a sponsorship view it affects us. Now is sponsorship season. I’m negotiating sponsors as we speak and everybody as put it on hold. Let’s just see how this plays out before we commit to anything. LINK: The Dusi is famous for the annual Canoe race but what is more important is the effect on the community that lines it’s banks for many kilometres. In many ways this river is their lifeblood. Ray de Vries You know the Dusi river is 160kms between Pietermaritzburg and Durban. There’s a million people that live over there. Lots and lots of people. We call them the forgotten communities. They’re the last people to find out when something goes wrong. Sibosisu Their livestock, some showed us they’re dying along the river because they drank this water. They had no other option except to have this kind of water as they rely on the river. V/O: Sibosisu Ntinga works closely with DUCT and assists with monitoring the Dusi river in the more rural areas. He says the people of villages like Nkanyezini are severely affected by the spill in the river. In their gardens they’re now complaining saying that their vegetables, as they put water on, are now starting dying. They’re showing illness from this dirty water. DORIS: Lucky You know, Derek, this has been a shock to our community. Especially because this is a rural area. Our people depend a lot on getting information when disasters like this take place. V/O Lucky Dlamini is the spokesperson for the Kwa-Ximba conservancy that was established in 2013 to help protect the biodiversity of the area. Lucky Derek: Has the government done much to spread the word? There’s a lot happening but you still feel that there’s not enough information on the ground. We think that our Environmental Affairs department should be doing something. They should be with us on the ground all the time. LINK: All fingers point to the KZN Department of the environment who should be standing up telling the affected community and the media about this spill and what is being done about it. V/O But the information is not forthcoming, and they only sent us a pre-recorded video statement by the KZN MEC for Economic Development, Tourism and Environmental Affairs, filmed earlier last week. Nomusa Dube-Ncube: We’ve heard about the unfortunate incident of spillage in the Umzinduzi river. We want to make sure that there has been compliance with the rules of the environmental act and we’ll ensure that those rules are adhered to. If there is any breach in terms of compliance we will have to make sure that whomever has breached the compliance will have to be fined or will have to be charged V/O: In Willowton’s written response the state that: We deeply regret the accident, and as is our responsibility we are doing everything possible to contain, clean-up and remediate the affected environment and assist the impacted community. V/O: In the meantime, the big question is how long will it take for the river to recover. There is talk of restocking the river, but Graham believes that given time the ecosystem might prove to be resilient... Dr Mark Graham What we are looking at it what are the tributaries going to give us which haven’t been impacted that we can actually utilise and inoculum back into the system to bring life back into this river. Dr Mark Graham Derek: Mark, spotlight on the Dusi, but surely nationally it’s just becoming a crisis with our rivers getting polluted? It’s an absolute crisis Derek and I think these sort of incidents bring the focus on it but what we need is a longer term solution. Dave Still Worldwide urban river are a big threat. Some countries are getting it right - others not so much. So, it’s a big challenge. Compared to some of the environmental problems in the world this is one of the more solvable ones. It’s really just a case of priorities and political will. PROMO 1 11” A massive ACCIDENTAL toxic spill into the Dusi river in KZN, has killed thousands of tonnes of fish and shocked the local communities. What is the future of the Dusi? PROMO 2 11” THE ACCIDENTAL SPILLAGE OF 1.6 million litres of vegetable oil and caustic soda into the iconic Dusi, has left communities in shock, and the future of the river in the balance. PROMO 3 11” Thousands of tonnes of dead fish have been removed from the Umzimduzi river in KZN following an ACCIDENTAL industrial spill. Who will take responsibility for this disaster? Pandora Long The human connections to rivers is far more deep than just ecologies, we are connected through an ecological cycle. Everything we do ends up in the river, it’s our water that we drink, but deeper than that it’s our cultural connection. The ceremony we have like our picnic is similar to ceremonies that they have in zulu cultures, celebrating life, celebrating the river... Dr Mark Graham This is a little symptom and a pimple on the surface which has just burst and created all this interest, but really as a community, as a society we want to be looking at the longer, bigger picture… and sustainably. Dr Mark Graham He’s collected a sample here from the stones insects. And he’s now just transferring that sample into a tray and we’re going to look and see what aquatic insect life is still in this river system. Dr Mark Graham So like the fish and you and I, the aquatic life is very dependent on the dissolved oxygen in the water. So that’s available oxygen that they’re using for breathing. If there’s none of that they’re going to be highly impacted. A spill like this is often associated with the depletion of the oxygen and that is probably largely what we’re seeing by way of all the dead fish. So, we’re looking at the insects now to see how they are being affected by this as well. Derek: And what have you found so far? We’re finding impacted sites and certainly immediately downstream of the spill was a significant reduction in life. Jean, I think there was one Olego Keat… one of the leeches. So, it’s a leech - a tough as old boots aquatic life form - often associated with highly polluted water. And that was the only thing that was alive. Dr Mark Graham What most people don’t realise is the complexity… we appreciate the wildlife at the game reserve when we see the grass and we see the wildebeest and so on - elephants and tigers and lions… But it’s exactly that same ecosystem that we’ve got here in the water and many things feeding on each other and being dependent on each other. So if one of those components is eliminated it has a cascade effect through the aquatic food web. Dave Still Being a big industry, doing the kind of work they do they’ve always been quite a high risk. And it’s one of the industries that does from time to time I think affect the sewage plant. Dave Still With the spill, some of that effluent went down the sewers, and the nature, being the caustic and the oils … that would have given the natural processes in the sewage plant a shock which basically give a big wow. After a few days I understand they’ve pretty much got it back right again. It hit it pretty hard for a few days. Derek: Could’ve been far worse? Yes it could have been. Ray de Vries Derek: Ray, what does the Dusi river mean to the people living in the valley? Ray de Vries: The Dusi unfortunately is synonymous with Dusi guts and bad water and all the rest. Maritzburg is just a seeping sewer and that’s where all the big problem is.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The worst disaster in more than 3 decades -- can the Dusi river recover from a devastating caustic soda and oil spill?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: At 4am on the 13th of August a storage tank filled with cooking oil crumbled, taking down with it a second container filled with caustic soda. This happened at the Willowton Plant in Pietermaritzburg, KZN. The alkaline mix flowed down the Bain spruit and into the Dusi river. It is estimated that 1.6 million litres of oil and caustic soda ended up in the river and by the weekend the milky polluted water had entered the Inanda dam outside Durban. The liquid is suffocating fish and other aquatic animals. The water is undrinkable for the communities and their animals. According to environmentalists it will take the Dusi several decades to recover.
metadata.Summary: The Mzunduzi (Dusi) river is famous because of the canoe marathon that is held on the river each year. It is the biggest canoeing event on the African continent, and one of the world’s most popular river marathons, attracting between 1600 and 2000 paddlers each year. But the river has also often been in the news for other reasons. Water quality has often been an issue and high e.coli counts are regularly measured. There are many rural communities who live along the banks of the river between PMB and Durban. On Tuesday 13 Aug there was a large oil and caustic soda spillage in PMB at the Willowton factory. 1.6 million litres of pollutants entered the Bain spruit and flowed into the Dusi river. The pollutants have had a devastating effect on the river, fish and other animals that depend on it. There are reports of dying cattle and massive fish die-offs all the way downstream to the Inanda dam.Provincial Government has issued a warning saying that people and animals should stay clear of the river. No-one should drink from the river, use it for irrigation or even paddle on it. The spill has been labelled the worst in 30 years. The Dusi Marathon organisers are concerned about the long-term effects on the river. The Dusi Umgeni Conservation Trust has stepped in to help monitor the water quality and assist in clean-up operations. Willowton has subcontracted 2 companies to help with the clean-up and government is also "working around the clock" but experts are saying that this kind of spill is very difficult to clean up. The caustic soda mixed with the oil has created a soapy substance that is suffocating all aquatic life in the river. Umgeni Water has tried to flush the river by opening the sluice of Henley Dam and although the water is running clear at some places, the damage has been done. Msunduzi Municipality spokesperson Thobeka Mafumbatha said the city’s environmental health unit was investigating the incident.
metadata.Further information: Caustic soda is corrosive and can cause burns to living tissue. Combined with fatty oils it becomes soapy, making a river clean-up exceptionally difficult. Water specialist Dr Anthony Turton from the Centre for Environmental Management at the University of Free State said the clean-up could take several years if the pollution spreads all the way down to Inanda Dam. Another leading environmental consultant and river specialist, Pandora Long, agreed. Nearly all aquatic life in a conservancy area along the river has been wiped out, according to Long. Turton says water-use licences for industrial users requires the use of berms or bunds to contain spills of hazardous liquids, as well as formal reporting to the regulating authorities at specified intervals along with site inspections. “This incident provides evidence of failure of the regulatory process,” said Turton.
